explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The rider has a bow and a crown, and the text says he "…rode out to overcome and conquer." John sees this right after the Lamb opens the first seal and a living creature calls out "Come!" I'll be honest, I came out of a junk drawer with way less to show for myself than a crown.

explanations.answer: To make peace with the nations
explanations.explanation: Nice thought, friend, and I'd love to bake cookies for that treaty signing. But the text says something different. The rider holds a bow, is given a crown, and rides out "…to overcome and conquer." Peace doesn't come up for this horse.

A harvest would be a lovely picture, but that's not what this rider is up to. He holds a bow and is given a crown. The text says he rides out "…to overcome and conquer." Nothing about gathering anything in.

Peace is right. The rider on the bright red horse is granted permission to take away peace from the earth and to make men slay one another. He's also given a great sword. This is a heavy picture, so I'm not going to joke about the horse.

I can see why you'd reach for joy, friend. It's a big word and I love it too. But the text says the rider is granted permission to take away peace from the earth (Revelation 6:4). Joy isn't named for this horse.

Hope is a good guess, and it's one I'd want to hold on to. Still, the text doesn't say it here. The red horse's rider is granted permission to take away peace from the earth. I think hope is a word worth keeping close while you read on.

True. Along with permission to take away peace, the text says the red horse's rider "…was given a great sword." It's the second seal, and the second living creature has just said "Come!" I think this is one of the heavy parts, so I'll just say it plainly.

This one's actually true, friend. The text says the rider on the bright red horse "…was given a great sword." It comes right after he's granted permission to take away peace from the earth. Easy one to second guess, since the whole scene is so big.

Yes, prices. The voice says, "A quart of wheat for a denarius, and three quarts of barley for a denarius, and do not harm the oil and wine." A denarius is a coin. The rider is holding scales, and the voice is counting out what the grain costs.

Good try, friend, but no tribes get called out here. The voice talks about grain. It says a quart of wheat for a denarius, and three quarts of barley for a denarius. Then it adds, "…do not harm the oil and wine."

explanations.answer: Words of praise to the Lamb
explanations.explanation: Praise to the Lamb is a lovely thought, friend, but it's not what the voice says here. After the black horse and its scales, the voice talks about wheat and barley and what they cost. It also says not to harm the oil and wine.

Death is the name. The rider on the pale green horse is named Death, and Hades follows close behind. They're given authority over a fourth of the earth. It's a heavy name, so I'll just say it plainly and let it sit.

Legion is a name from a different story, baker. It's the name a man with unclean spirits gives in Mark 5:9. On the pale green horse, the text says the rider's name is Death. Hades follows close behind him.
Wormwood isn't the rider here, baker. The text says the pale green horse's rider is named Death. Hades follows close behind. It's a rough name, I know, but that's what John says.
Close, but he isn't alone. The text says Hades followed close behind Death. Both of them were given authority over a fourth of the earth. So the answer is False, and that detail is easy to miss.

False is right. John says Death is the rider's name, and then adds that Hades followed close behind. They were given authority over a fourth of the earth together. It's a heavy detail, and a careful reading catches it.

explanations.answer: For the word of God and their testimony
explanations.explanation: That's what the text says. John sees the souls of those who had been slain "…for the word of God and for the testimony they had upheld." They're under the altar. I think this is one of the quietest, most serious spots in the whole passage.

explanations.answer: For breaking the laws of their nation
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. The text gives a different reason. They had been slain "…for the word of God and for the testimony they had upheld." Nothing about breaking laws comes up.

explanations.answer: For fighting in the armies of the king
explanations.explanation: Armies aren't in this scene. John sees souls under the altar, and he says they were slain "…for the word of God and for the testimony they had upheld." That's the reason the text gives. A soldier's story is a different one.

Right. Each of them is given a white robe and told to rest a little while longer. The text says that's until the full number of their fellow servants, their brothers, were killed, just as they had been killed. A white robe and a little rest, and I think that's a kind thing to hand someone.

explanations.answer: Go down and judge the earth
explanations.explanation: Close to what they asked, friend, but not what they were told. They cried out, "How long, O Lord, holy and true, until You judge those who dwell upon the earth and avenge our blood?" The answer they got was a white robe and to rest a little while longer. Nobody sends them down to do the judging.

explanations.answer: Sing a new song to the Lamb
explanations.explanation: A new song does get sung in Revelation 5:9, but not here. In this scene, each soul is given a white robe and told to rest a little while longer. That's what the text says, baker. I think it's a gentle thing to hand someone.

That's it. After the great earthquake, "…the sun became black like sackcloth of goat hair…" The whole moon also turned blood red. Sackcloth of goat hair is rough, dark cloth. I'd say that's a sky nobody's going to forget.

explanations.answer: It stands still in the sky
explanations.explanation: Standing still is a different moment, in Joshua 10:13. Joshua was Israel's leader, and that happened in his day. In the sixth seal, the text says the sun "…became black like sackcloth of goat hair…" That's the picture John gives us.

I wish I could give you a brighter ending, friend, but the text goes the other way. After the great earthquake, "…the sun became black like sackcloth of goat hair…" That's the dark picture John sees. Hold on, though, because this story isn't finished.
True. When the Lamb opens the sixth seal, John says "…the whole moon turned blood red…" That comes right alongside the sun going black. Quite a sky, and I should know, since I have one of my own.
It's True, friend. John says that when the sixth seal is opened, "…the whole moon turned blood red…" The sun becomes black like sackcloth of goat hair too. It's a lot to take in.
Scroll is right. John says, "The sky receded like a scroll being rolled up…" I think that's the picture he wants us to hold on to. Every mountain and island is moved from its place, too.
A curtain is a fair thought, friend, since it also pulls back. But the text uses a different word. It says the sky "…receded like a scroll being rolled up…" Scroll is the word to keep.
A tent folds up too, so I get it, baker. But John doesn't use that comparison. He says the sky "…receded like a scroll being rolled up…" Scroll is the word.
True. John says the sky receded, "…and every mountain and island was moved from its place." Mountains look pretty settled to me, and these moved. I think that tells you how big this moment is.

It's True, friend. After the sky recedes like a scroll being rolled up, John says, "…every mountain and island was moved from its place." Not one of them stays put. A tricky one to doubt, because mountains seem so steady.

Caves it is. John says they "…hid in the caves and among the rocks of the mountains." That's kings, nobles, commanders, the rich, the mighty, and every slave and free man, all hiding in the same spots.
You picked a tall place, but towers aren't in this scene. The text says they "…hid in the caves and among the rocks of the mountains." I think a cave is a lot less comfortable for a king.

Palaces would be a nice place to hide, friend, but the text puts them somewhere else. The kings and everyone with them "…hid in the caves and among the rocks of the mountains." There's no palace in sight.

explanations.answer: The One on the throne and the Lamb
explanations.explanation: That's what they say. They cry out, "…hide us from the face of the One seated on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb." Notice who is named. It's the One on the throne and the Lamb, not the horses.

explanations.answer: The four riders on the horses
explanations.explanation: The riders came earlier, so I see why you'd think of them. But the people never name them here. They call out, "…hide us from the face of the One seated on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb." That's who they're hiding from.

The souls under the altar show up earlier, but the hiding people don't mention them. In their cry, they say, "…hide us from the face of the One seated on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb." That is the answer the text gives. Good try, baker.
Not quite, friend. They don't say they can withstand it. They say, "For the great day of Their wrath has come, and who is able to withstand it?" That's a question they ask. So False is the answer.
False is right. The people hiding don't boast. They say, "…the great day of Their wrath has come, and who is able to withstand it?" It's a question they ask while they hide in the caves and rocks.
